principles.rule: Dry rosés are made mostly from Grenache, Carignan, Mourvèdre and Cabernets; serve around 55F, off-dry blush colder.
Only one star should shine: show off a special bottle with simpler food, or a showpiece dish with a lower-key wine.
Echoing a flavor (mint in wine and dish) is not a guarantee; pairings hinge on measurable tastes, not flavor descriptors.
Wines taste different with food than alone; critics' 'good with pasta' notes are often untested guesses.
Pairings work by likeness (off-dry Riesling with apricot-chutney pork) or by contrast (crisp Sauvignon Blanc cutting briny oysters).
Acidity is the most important pairing factor: a tart wine cuts rich, salty, oily, creamy, fried or mildly spicy dishes like a lemon wedge.
Tart dishes (vinaigrettes, capers, tomatoes, leeks) need a wine at least as tart, or the wine tastes thin.
Sharp, simple wines make pristine ingredients like sweet corn, heirloom tomatoes, fresh crab and mozzarella taste brighter.
Low-acid wines are hard to pair; give them mild food with a touch of lemon or tang.
Some sweetness in wine tames moderate chili heat, as with Korean barbecued chicken or twice-cooked pork.
Off-dry wines echo fruit chutneys, salsas and sauces made with fresh or dried fruit.
Sweet wine contrasts salt, the logic behind Sauternes with Roquefort and Port with Stilton.
A dessert wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it tastes sour; dry brut fails with frosted wedding cake.
Acidity reduces perceived saltiness; whites and sparkling usually beat reds with salty food.
Tannin amplifies salt, and salt or chili heat makes alcohol taste hotter.
Salty food loves off-dry or sweet wine; the salt-sweet contrast is time-tested.
A pinch of salt on the food can sometimes revive a flat-tasting pairing.
Bitter, grilled or charred foods and bitter greens suit tannic reds.
Fat and protein in rare red meat or cheese soften tannin; low-protein vegetarian dishes make tannic reds harsher.
Hard, sharp cheeses (aged Parmesan, Manchego, aged Cheddar, goat cheese) can make tannic reds taste metallic.
Tannic red with oily fish gives a metallic taste; choose low-tannin reds like Pinot Noir for fish.
Food magnifies oak; match oaky wines with grilled, smoked or caramelized food that shares those flavors.
Unoaked or lightly oaked wines are the most flexible at the table.
Oak adds a round texture that suits cream sauces, compound butters and slow braises.
Match weight: light wines with light dishes, rich wines with rich dishes.
The higher the alcohol, the fewer foods a wine suits; medium-bodied wines (11-13%) are easiest.
Slow-cooked garlic and onions add sweetness and link to riper, oaked or earthy European wines.
Green olives tilt a dish toward white wine; black olives toward Merlot, Cabernet or Syrah.
Cured meats like prosciutto, bacon or pancetta let fish, poultry and pork take soft reds or rosés.
A little goat cheese, feta or Gorgonzola bridges salads and vegetables to high-acid whites.
Delicate herbs (chervil, dill, tarragon) favor Riesling and Chardonnay; pungent herbs favor Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Cabernet.
Legumes go white with herbs or red with pork products; fish on green lentils can take red wine.
Dark or dried mushrooms make food red-wine friendly; pale creamy mushrooms favor textured whites.
Toasted nuts echo oak-aged wines; skin-on nuts soften tannin perception.
Cooking method matters: steaming and poaching are low impact; grilling, smoking and blackening transform the wine choice.
The sauce usually dictates the wine; match its dominant taste (acid, sweet, heat) rather than the protein.
Butter, cream and emulsified sauces pair with rich-textured whites like Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Viognier.
Strongly flavored side dishes can matter more than the main ingredient when choosing the wine.
Cook only with wine you would drink; cooked wine loses its identity, so save fine wine for last-minute additions.
Avoid very oaky or tannic wines in cooking; they add bitterness.
Use a juicy fruity red such as Rioja joven, Beaujolais or Dolcetto for sangria.
Tart wine: serve with rich, creamy, fatty, salty or tart food; it can replace the lemon wedge.
High-alcohol wine: needs weighty food; avoid very spicy or salty dishes.
Tannic wine: serve protein and fat, black pepper, bitter vegetables or grilled food; avoid spicy heat.
Oaky wine: use bold dishes with nuts, sweet spice, grilling or smoking and rich textured sauces.
Aged reds: show them with rare meat and simple preparations, not complex recipes.
Aged whites: echo nuts, sherry and dried fruit, and add acidity to the dish with lemon or verjus.
Tart food: avoid reds except sharp ones (Sangiovese, Pinot Noir, Gamay); consider dry rosé and sparkling.
Slightly sweet food: choose Chenin Blanc, Riesling or sake, or a very ripe young dry wine.
Salty food: choose low-alcohol wines with some sweetness and little oak or tannin.
Spicy food: young, low-alcohol, unoaked off-dry whites, rosés or sparkling; for fiery dishes drink beer instead.
Bitter food: choose oaky or tannic wines, or failing that high-acid ones.
Food served very hot exaggerates alcohol; let it cool or serve chilled wines.
Sparkling suits fried food, pastry, butter, salt, cream, oily fish, caviar, raw fish and moderate heat thanks to bubbles and acidity.
Toasty, nutty Champagne-style bubbly suits sautéed dishes and toasty elements like grains, nuts and corn.
Fruit-forward New World sparkling suits Indian, Thai, Vietnamese, Latin and Caribbean dishes.
Bubbly rescues hard matches like eggs and soups, and rustic dishes like polenta, pesto and hummus.
Sparkling struggles with very rich or very spicy dishes, sweet desserts (unless a sweet style), bitter vegetables and rich red meat.
Chardonnay is easily lost behind strong or bold dishes; pair with food enhanced by its round, silky texture.
With buttery malolactic Chardonnay, cook with butter; with oaky versions, use toasted nuts, nut oils, plank roasting or braising.
Chardonnay makes an ideal first-course wine.
Sauvignon Blanc is one of the best food wines; even people who dislike it alone enjoy it with a meal.
Classic unoaked Sauvignon Blanc highlights a dish without masking it; ideal for steamed or simple preparations.
Oaky 'Chardonnay wannabe' Sauvignon Blancs should be paired following Chardonnay rules.
Aged Sauvignon Blanc loses its green zest; pair it with more pungent fish, strong sauces or textured vegetarian dishes.
Sauvignon Blanc is a great starter wine, letting the meal progress from lighter whites to reds.
Soften a vinaigrette for wine by using citrus, verjus or the wine itself instead of vinegar.
Riesling may be the most versatile white for food; its range comes mainly from sweetness level.
Match Riesling's weight to the food: riper Australian or Californian versions for richer dishes, lighter German ones for delicate.
Bone-dry Riesling can replace a squeeze of lemon or lime on a dish.
Riesling is one of the few wines that handles egg dishes such as quiche.
Pick the right Riesling: bone-dry for oysters; off-dry for spice, sweetness, smoked foods.
With Pinot Gris, style matters most: crisp Italian versions act like Sauvignon Blanc; rich Alsace versions like Chardonnay.
Drink Pinot Grigio/Gris young, within about two years; only Alsace versions improve for up to a decade.
Serve Italian-style Pinot Grigio cool; oilier styles lose flavor if served too cold.
Gewürztraminer's 'spicy' name misleads: its high alcohol clashes with chili heat; it suits sweet spices instead.
Gewürztraminer with Chinese food is not a guaranteed match; use off-dry styles for sweet or mildly spicy dishes.
Gewürztraminer's bold personality can need high-impact cooking: smoked, grilled, even blackened foods.
Drink Viognier young, when its stone-fruit exuberance is strongest; aged ones turn nutty and marmalade-like.
Viognier combines Chardonnay's texture, Sauvignon's balanced acidity and aromatic Riesling/Gewürz flavors; underrated with food.
Viognier likes cooking that brings out sweetness (slow roasting, caramelizing, smoking, frying); avoid heavy grilling or blackening.
Cabernet can crush delicate dishes; its tannin, alcohol and oak need food with fat, protein and character.
Starch does not soften tannin; fat does, so butter and dairy help with Cabernet.
Big wine with big cheese usually fails; Cabernet suits mild to moderate cheeses, never blue cheese.
Bordeaux's earthy, cedar notes allow fresh herbs, mushrooms and sharp vegetables like eggplant and chard.
Show mature Cabernet with simple dishes: plain beef stew, pot roast, grilled veal or lamb chop.
Older Cabernet with rarer meat; young juicy Cabernet with long-cooked meats and stews.
Black pepper tames young Cabernet's tannin; with older wines, cut back the pepper.
Most chocolate is too sweet for dry red; bittersweet chocolate in a mole can suit ripe New World Cabernet.
Merlot comes in soft, medium and Cabernet-like styles; ask before buying, since the bottle may not be the easy wine you expect.
Treat big Merlot like Cabernet and soft Merlot like Pinot Noir, including with fish.
Merlot's herbal, earthy streak handles fennel, eggplant, radicchio, chard and broccoli better than Cabernet; choose leaner European styles.
Tart marinades (yogurt, tarragon, thyme, pomegranate) suit Merlot's relatively high acidity.
Throw rosemary branches on the grill fire to echo herbal notes in Merlot.
Pinot Noir is the most food-friendly red: low tannin, high acidity, a white wine in red clothing.
Pinot Noir is the great equalizer when diners order fish, fowl and meat at one table.
Avoid heavy cream, butter or fat with Pinot Noir; they swamp its subtlety.
Show older Pinot Noir with simple leg of lamb, roast veal loin or coq au vin.
Serve Pinot Noir slightly chilled as a picnic wine with cold cuts and mild cheese.
Middle Eastern dishes generally pair well with both Pinot Noir and Syrah.
Sangiovese's moderate alcohol, sharp acidity and balanced tannin make it one of the most food-flexible reds.
Chianti with tomato-sauced pasta and pizza is a cliché because it reliably works: tomato acid meets wine acid.
Treat Super Tuscan blends and Brunello like bigger, tannic reds, though their zip handles more herbs and spice than pure Cabernet.
Sangiovese has enough body and acid for rich slow braises that would overwhelm Pinot Noir.
Deglazing with wine or wine and lemon makes pan sauces that suit Sangiovese and Pinot Noir.
Petite Sirah is a different grape from Syrah.
Syrah's high alcohol buries subtle dishes; it likes coarse textures like polenta, black beans and grainy mustard.
Echo Syrah's pepper with spice and pepper in marinades, glazes and condiments.
As Syrah matures it behaves like Cabernet; pair it the same way.
Sour cream can make some wines taste metallic; choose full-bodied wine with an acidic edge.
Zinfandel comes as off-dry white Zin, light Beaujolais-like red, claret-style red and big 'monster' red; style decides the pairing.
Old-vine Zinfandel is more concentrated and complex.
Treat white Zinfandel like off-dry Riesling, with less acidity and more alcohol.
Chill light, juicy red Zinfandel to bring out fruit, especially in warm weather.
Zinfandel loves grilling, barbecue, slow smoking and braises; poaching and steaming don't suit red Zin.
Drink white Zinfandel young; aged red Zin behaves like mature Cabernet or Merlot.
Artichokes distort wine when they dominate, but sautéed as a supporting ingredient they add nuttiness.
Botrytis (noble rot) concentrates sugar while keeping acidity; recognize it by a honeyed note.
The one hard rule: a dessert wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it tastes sour.
Late-harvest wines pair best with fruit desserts that echo their fruit: stone fruit, apples, pears, sweet citrus.
Oaky dessert wines suit butterscotch, caramel, toffee, crème brûlée; honey echoes botrytis.
Don't serve chocolate to show off Sauternes or TBA; chocolate and mocha belong with Port and Banyuls.
Adding fruit (berry jam, cherry sauce) to chocolate desserts helps them pair with dessert wines.
Simple summer fruit on shortcake or phyllo is the ideal stage for sweet sparkling wine; avoid heavy buttercream.
Hazelnuts are the most wine-flexible nut, then almonds and walnuts.
Berry and citrus combinations suit virtually all off-dry to sweet sparkling wines.
Decide your priority: choose the wine first and plan the menu, or let a special dish dictate the wine.
Bread and cheese fill flavor and texture gaps in any menu.
Offer more than one wine so guests can choose.
When in doubt, serve a region's food with its local wine; it works nine times in ten.
Dining out: if a dish is the priority, choose wine around it; ask what the restaurant is known for.
Drink a glass of water for each glass of wine when tasting several wines with a meal.
Austere, lean wines can be unpleasant alone yet supply a welcome contrast to rich dishes.
Very complex wines are often best on their own or with simple food; complicated recipes hide their subtleties.
Thin, light, bland foods are hard to pair because almost any wine dominates them.
